modules.title: Java Introduction & Environment Setup
modules.objective: Install or select the JDK, understand the compiler/runtime workflow, and run a real Java program.
prerequisites: Java Development Kit (JDK) installed; IntelliJ IDEA or a terminal and text editor.

modules.finalOutcome: A Java source file was compiled and executed. You can repeat the same example from a terminal or IntelliJ.
conceptOverview: Java is a general-purpose programming language. You write instructions in a .java source file; the Java compiler checks the source and translates it into bytecode stored in .class files. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs that bytecode. This separation makes the same compiled program usable on different supported operating systems.

The Java Development Kit (JDK) includes the compiler (javac), the java launcher, and other tools. IntelliJ IDEA is an editor and development environment; it helps you write and run code, but the JDK is what actually compiles and executes the program.
modules.whyItMatters: Before learning variables or classes, you must be able to compile and run a known working program. When an error occurs, understanding whether it came from the compiler, the runtime, or your own code saves time.
modules.realLifeExample: Imagine building the first version of a hospital registration application. You start with a tiny program that prints a message, verify your environment, and then gradually add patient information and application features.

coreIdeas.explanation: Human-readable Java instructions that you create and edit.
Checks Java syntax and types, then produces bytecode in a .class file.
The JVM executes compiled bytecode; java is the command that starts the program.
The entry point for this ordinary command-line example. Java begins here and executes statements in order.
Displays text on the terminal and moves to the next line.

learningTakeaways: Java source is compiled before the JVM runs it.
Class names, filenames and main must be used correctly in a basic console program.
Small changes followed by another run help you understand cause and effect.

conceptOverview: A variable is a named place to store a value while a program runs. Every Java variable has a type: for example, int stores whole numbers, double stores floating-point numbers, boolean stores true or false, and String represents text. Java checks that operations are consistent with the declared types.

Operators combine or compare values. Arithmetic operators such as * and + perform calculations; assignment with = stores a result in a variable. A program becomes useful when it can accept values, calculate something, and show the result.
modules.whyItMatters: Real applications work with different kinds of information. A student registration form needs text for the student name, whole numbers for courses and credits, decimal values for fees, and a true/false value for enrollment.
modules.realLifeExample: A university fee estimator can multiply the number of courses by credits per course, then multiply total credits by the fee for each credit. The output should explain the calculated values, not just print a bare number.

learningTakeaways: Use an appropriate type for each value.
Compute intermediate values in named variables to keep logic readable.

conceptOverview: A condition is an expression that evaluates to true or false. A program uses if/else, the conditional (ternary) operator, or switch to select which action or result should be used. A loop repeats a section of code until its work is finished.

For a collection of marks, repetition is more reliable than manually writing a separate addition for every student. In the example, a for-each loop calculates the total, and a chained conditional expression chooses the grade based on the average.
modules.whyItMatters: Student grading, menu choices, stock checks, and access decisions all require different actions depending on data. Loops help process an entire group without copying the same statement many times.
modules.realLifeExample: A course result system receives several marks. It totals them, calculates the average, and chooses A, B, C, or F according to its grading rules. A separate menu chooses Add, View, or Exit based on the selected option.

modules.whyItMatters: Searching for an ID or cleaning up a name should not require rewriting a loop or text operation everywhere in a real application. A reusable method makes the behavior consistent for every caller.
modules.realLifeExample: In a university registration program, a search method can locate a student score in an array, while a name-normalization method removes accidental spaces from form input before comparing entries.

Ends a method and gives the result back to the caller.

learningTakeaways: Give each method a clear, single responsibility.
Array indexes begin at zero; always consider the not-found case.
String methods typically return new text rather than editing an existing String.

conceptOverview: A class is a blueprint that describes the data and behavior of objects. An object is one particular instance created from that class. For example, a Student class defines the fields and methods common to students; each Student object stores its own name and credit count.

Encapsulation means keeping a class’s state under its control. In Java, private fields block direct changes from other classes, while constructors and methods can check whether proposed values are valid. This protects rules such as “credits cannot be negative.”
modules.whyItMatters: In a real student or hospital system, arbitrary code must not be able to put invalid values into an important record. Encapsulation gives the application one clear place to validate updates and keep each object consistent.
modules.realLifeExample: A student enrollment system creates a Student object with a name and 15 credits. Later the user registers another course, so the application updates credits through a method that checks the new number before storing it.

coreIdeas.explanation: A class defines the structure; an object is a concrete item with its own field values.
Runs when new creates an object; it establishes the object’s initial state.
Can be accessed directly only from within its declaring class.
Methods used to read a value or update it under controlled rules.
Refers to the current object, distinguishing a field from a parameter with the same name.
A field whose reference/value cannot be reassigned after construction.

learningTakeaways: A class describes; an object holds actual values.
Constructors initialize valid objects.
Private fields and validated methods protect data from accidental invalid changes.

modules.finalOutcome: You can reuse common class structure while selecting behavior through interfaces.
conceptOverview: Inheritance lets one class reuse or specialize behavior from a parent class. An interface describes a capability that different classes promise to provide. Polymorphism lets one piece of code use objects with different implementations through a shared parent or interface type.

The example has a Payable interface, an abstract Employee parent class, and two concrete employee types. Both know how to calculate pay, but use different values. The caller needs only the common Payable method.
modules.whyItMatters: Without a shared interface, a payroll program may require a different if statement for every employee type. Polymorphism lets the payroll loop call one method and rely on each object to perform its own calculation.
modules.realLifeExample: A hospital has permanent employees and contract workers. Both must receive payment, but their payment rules may differ. A payroll service can process any Payable worker without knowing the specific employee type.

coreIdeas.explanation: Makes a class inherit from another class.
Declares that a class provides the methods required by an interface.
A base class that can share code but cannot be instantiated directly.
Marks a method as an implementation or override of an inherited/interface method.
When an interface reference invokes a method, Java chooses the concrete object’s implementation at runtime.

learningTakeaways: Inheritance reuses a parent class’s members.
Interfaces define common capabilities shared by different classes.
Polymorphism simplifies client code by removing type-specific branching.

modules.finalOutcome: You can diagnose and handle predictable invalid-input conditions while preserving useful error information.
conceptOverview: An exception is an object that describes a problem encountered while a program runs. Some problems should interrupt normal execution, such as invalid input or a missing file. Java uses throw to signal an exception and try/catch to handle a specific exception without necessarily ending the whole program.

Debugging means observing what the program is doing and finding why it behaves incorrectly. A debugger can pause execution at a breakpoint, show variable values, and advance through statements one at a time.
modules.whyItMatters: Applications should reject invalid data clearly instead of silently accepting it or crashing without explanation. For example, a hospital form should not accept an impossible patient age.
modules.realLifeExample: A registration system reads an age. It accepts 20, rejects -4 with a meaningful message, then continues processing 35. The program should recover from one invalid entry and still handle the remaining data.

coreIdeas.explanation: Creates and raises an exception at the point where the problem is detected.
A standard exception for an invalid argument passed to a method.
Tries an operation and handles a matching exception if one occurs.
Retrieves the explanatory message from the caught exception.
A debugger marker that pauses execution so variables and control flow can be inspected.

learningTakeaways: Validate inputs where the rule is defined.
Catch only errors you can meaningfully handle.
Use a debugger to observe the exact values and branches involved in a problem.

Generics specify which types a collection or method accepts. For example, List<String> communicates that each element should be a String, helping the compiler detect accidental type mistakes before the program runs.
modules.whyItMatters: A project may need a list of registered users, a unique set of course names, or a lookup from course name to score. Choosing the right collection makes these operations simpler and more reliable.
modules.realLifeExample: A student enters Java, Python, and Java as chosen learning topics. The program keeps the original list, creates a unique set containing Java and Python, and looks up a numeric score for each course name.

learningTakeaways: Use a List for ordered, possibly repeated values.
Use a Set for uniqueness and a Map for key-based lookup.
Generics help the compiler enforce which types can be placed in collections.

conceptOverview: A thread is one path of execution within a running Java process. Concurrency means handling multiple tasks whose lifetimes overlap. On some systems tasks may run in parallel on different CPU cores; on others, the runtime interleaves them.

practicalSteps.title: Step 1 — Understand the documented pipeline

blocks.text: A push to main starts a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner, which checks out the code, logs in to Docker Hub, builds and pushes a tagged image, then connects to EC2 to replace the container. The runner and EC2 instance are different machines.

practicalSteps.title: Step 2 — Add the exact recorded GitHub Actions workflow

blocks.text: The complete YAML below is the original editable source from the CI/CD practical. The secrets and workflow action versions are preserved exactly as recorded.

blocks.label: ORIGINAL WORKFLOW — SPRING BOOT BUILD AND DEPLOY
blocks.text:
# Workflow name and trigger
name: Spring Boot Build and Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

# Application configuration
env:
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/spring-boot-app
  CONTAINER_NAME: spring-boot-app
  APP_PORT: 8080

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # 1. Get source code
      - name: Checkout Repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # 2. Login to Docker Hub
      - name: Docker Hub Login
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # 3. Build and push Docker image
      - name: Build and Push Image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # 4. Deploy to AWS EC2
      - name: Deploy to EC2
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.EC2_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.EC2_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.EC2_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            set -e

            # Pull the new image
            docker pull "${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}"

            # Remove the old container
            docker rm -f "${{ env.CONTAINER_NAME }}" 2>/dev/null || true

            # Run the updated container
            docker run -d \
              --name "${{ env.CONTAINER_NAME }}" \
              --restart unless-stopped \
              -p "${{ env.APP_PORT }}:8080" \
              "${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}"
